0.text: Could TikTok help your local business?
Treat it as a small test with a clear purpose, not a promise of customers.
Choose one service, one audience and one useful action you want a viewer to take.
Decide how much time you can spend before you start.

1.text: Start with a question customers already ask.
A repair shop could explain what information to bring when requesting an estimate.
A bakery could show how to place an advance order.
Use examples from your own work, explain the limits
and avoid presenting a demonstration as a guaranteed result.

2.text: State the area you actually serve and make the next step easy to understand.
A viewer should be able to tell what you offer and how to contact you.
Check the destination from a phone.
Do not assume someone watching a video is nearby or ready to buy.

3.text: Film one clear idea at a time.
Use understandable speech and readable captions, then preview the finished video on a phone.
Show your own materials and get permission before featuring customers.
A useful explanation is a practical starting point; it does not require copying an unrelated trend.

4.text: TikTok provides a Commercial Music Library for business content
but do not assume a song available in an app is cleared for every use.
Check the permitted use for each destination when sharing the same video elsewhere
and retain the rights evidence with your project.

5.text: Keep a simple record of the topic, posting date
production time and enquiries you can reasonably connect to the test.
Ask new customers how they found you without assuming every sale came from a video.
Views can help describe reach, but they do not establish local demand or profitable work.

6.text: What customer question could you answer first?
Review your test against the time spent and the useful responses received.
Continue the ideas that help people understand your business, revise confusing explanations
and stop formats that consume time without evidence of value.
